claim: Rules in Covent Garden is London's oldest restaurant, founded 1798 by Thomas Rule as an oyster bar, serving traditional British game cookery and frequented by Dickens, Thackeray, H.G. Wells, Chaplin and Olivier.
quote: Established in 1798 by Thomas Rule... London's oldest restaurant... hosted renowned writers including Charles Dickens, William Makepeace Thackeray, and H.G. Wells... legendary actors such as Henry Irving, Laurence Olivier, Buster Keaton, and Charlie Chaplin.

claim: Rules has private dining rooms named after Charles Dickens and Graham Greene, the latter featuring in Greene's novel The End of the Affair, and appears in works by Evelyn Waugh and John le Carre.
quote: a dining room named after Graham Greene which the novelist used when he visited London and which featured in his novel 'The End of the Affair'... Rules has also appeared in novels by Rosamond Lehmann, Evelyn Waugh, Graham Greene, John Le Carre.

claim: Simpson's Tavern, founded 1757 down a Dickensian City of London alley, is reputedly London's oldest chophouse and considered the melancholy tavern Scrooge visits in A Christmas Carol; after a forced 2022 closure the Cloth team acquired the Grade II building to reopen it mid-2026 as Cloth Cornhill.
quote: Simpson's Tavern's traditional British fare dates back to 1757... known affectionately as 'the oldest chophouse in London'... Many consider Simpson's Tavern to be the 'usual melancholy tavern' Ebenezer Scrooge visits in A Christmas Carol.

claim: The Witchery by the Castle, founded 1979 in Boswell's Court (a 1595 listed building at the gates of Edinburgh Castle), is a candlelit, oak-panelled gothic fine-dining room named for the witch burnings that took place on nearby Castlehill.
quote: Hidden in a collection of historic buildings dating back to 1595, at the gates of Edinburgh Castle, the Witchery is steeped in centuries of rich Scottish history... Lit exclusively by candlelight, the tapestry-draped main dining room is an ode to opulence.

claim: The Witchery takes its name from the hundreds of suspected witches burned at the stake on Castlehill near the restaurant during the 16th and 17th centuries.
quote: The name comes from the history of witch burnings in 16th and 17th century Scotland, many of which took place on the nearby Castlehill... hundreds of suspected witches were burned at the stake here in the 1600s.

claim: The Elephant House, a George IV Bridge tea-and-coffee house opened 1995 overlooking Edinburgh Castle, is famed as a spot where J.K. Rowling wrote early Harry Potter and where Ian Rankin and Alexander McCall Smith also worked.
quote: the place where J.K. Rowling wrote while 'overlooking Edinburgh Castle'... 'birthplace' of the Harry Potter series. The cafe has also attracted other notable authors like Ian Rankin and Alexander McCall-Smith.

claim: The Elephant House reopened in December 2025 after a major fire and now features a Writers' Room displaying Rowling's salvaged table.
quote: It reopened in December 2025 after a major fire and now includes a Writers' Room with Rowling's salvaged table.

claim: The Brazen Head on Bridge Street is Ireland's oldest pub with a hostelry on the site since 1198, now a gastrobar serving Irish stew, fish and chips and Guinness with nightly Irish music.
quote: Established in 1198, making it 'Ireland's Oldest Pub.'... The Brazen Head is situated on Bridge Street in Dublin... reviews highlight their fish and chips, beef stew, and Guinness... Live Irish music plays nightly.

claim: The Brazen Head was a revolutionary hub where Oliver Bond and the United Irishmen plotted the 1798 rebellion and Robert Emmet planned his 1803 uprising, and Swift, Behan and Kavanagh are said to have drunk there.
quote: local resident Oliver Bond and his fellow United Irishmen met here to plot their rebellion in 1798, while Robert Emmet also used the bar to plan his uprising of 1803... Patrick Kavanagh, Brendan Behan and Jonathan Swift are all said to have drunk here.

claim: The Winding Stair on Ormond Quay, named after a W.B. Yeats poem and its twisting staircase, was a famed 1970s-80s writers' and artists' bookshop revived as a restaurant by Elaine Murphy in 2006 serving seasonal Irish produce above a still-operating Irish-literature bookshop overlooking the Ha'penny Bridge.
quote: Named after the Yeats poem, and in honour of its winding staircase... overlooking the river Liffey, with an iconic view of the Ha'penny bridge... In 2006, Elaine Murphy brought this much-loved spot back to life as a restaurant, championing seasonal, Irish produce.
